title: Gastroenteritis and urinary tract infection in children
blurb: Rehydrate a child with gastroenteritis safely using NICE CG84, and collect, test and act on urine for suspected UTI using NICE NG224.
question: Freddie, 2, weighs 12 kg and has had gastroenteritis for two days. He has dry mucous membranes and fewer wet nappies but is alert with no shock. What is the recommended oral rehydration plan?

teach.h: Two common illnesses, two safety jobs
teach.body: Gastroenteritis and urinary tract infection (UTI) are among the commonest reasons children see a nurse. Formally, NICE CG84 covers diarrhoea and vomiting caused by gastroenteritis in under 5s, and NICE NG224 covers UTI in under 16s. Plain English: in gastroenteritis your job is to prevent and correct dehydration and stop spread; in UTI your job is to get a clean urine sample, test it the right way for age and escalate the youngest babies at once.

teach.caption: Symptoms lasting longer than this are a reason for review, not reassurance.

head: Situation
Plan
rows: Offer ORS as a supplemental fluid
After rehydration, at risk of recurrence
Consider ORS 5 mL/kg after each large watery stool
Low-osmolarity ORS 50 mL/kg over 4 h plus maintenance
teach.caption: Give ORS little and often. Continue breastfeeding throughout. Avoid fruit juice and fizzy drinks.
Red flag signs of dehydration mean a child at risk of progressing to shock: review them often.

teach.body: Washing hands with soap in warm running water, and drying them carefully, is the most important way to stop gastroenteritis spreading: after the toilet or nappy changes and before preparing or eating food. Towels used by an infected child should not be shared. Children should stay away from school or childcare until 48 hours after the last episode of diarrhoea or vomiting, and should not swim in pools for 2 weeks after the last episode of diarrhoea.
teach.cite: NICE CG84 recs 1.8.2.1 and infection control

teach.h: Collecting urine in a young child

steps.label: Urine collection pad
steps.sub: If clean catch is not possible

steps.label: Send or refrigerate
steps.sub: Fridge or boric acid if culture not within 4 h

teach.caption: Do not use cotton wool balls, gauze or sanitary towels to collect urine (NG224).

head: Age
What to do
rows: Refer at once to a paediatric specialist; send urine
Dipstick: if either positive, culture and antibiotics
Dipstick (leukocyte esterase and nitrite) is as useful
teach.caption: Under 3 months with fever: parenteral antibiotics per NICE NG143.

teach.note: Atypical UTI (seriously ill, poor urine flow, abdominal mass, raised creatinine, septicaemia, no response in 48 h, non-E. coli) needs ultrasound during the acute infection.

teach.text: Do not wait for a dipstick in a baby under 3 months. NG224 says refer immediately to a paediatric specialist and send urine for microscopy and culture. Dipstick testing starts at 3 months, and it is from 3 years that a dipstick is as useful as microscopy and culture.

teach.h: Scenario: Freddie, 2, in the children's assessment unit
teach.body: Freddie weighs 12 kg, has dry mucous membranes and fewer wet nappies but is alert and warm with a normal CRT. Nurse Grace recognises clinical dehydration without shock. She plans low-osmolarity ORS 50 mL/kg over 4 hours (600 mL) plus maintenance, offered in small frequent sips, and encourages his mother to keep breastfeeding. She reviews him regularly for red flag signs and teaches handwashing before he goes home.

items: Clinical dehydration: ORS 50 mL/kg over 4 hours plus maintenance, little and often.
Shock: IV 0.9% sodium chloride 10 mL/kg rapidly, then reassess.
Off school or childcare until 48 hours after the last episode; no swimming for 2 weeks.
Urine: clean catch first, then pads; never cotton wool or gauze.
Under 3 months with suspected UTI: refer immediately to a paediatric specialist.

summary: You can now rehydrate a child with gastroenteritis using the CG84 plan, spot the move from dehydration to shock and give exclusion advice. You can also collect, test and act on urine for suspected UTI by age using NG224.

A.q: Poppy, 3, has gastroenteritis. Her last episode of diarrhoea was on Monday at 10:00. When can she return to nursery?
A.why: Children should be kept away from school or childcare until 48 hours after the last episode of diarrhoea or vomiting: Wednesday at 10:00.

whyNot.0: Twelve hours is too short; the exclusion period is 48 hours.
whyNot.1: Twenty-four hours is half the recommended 48-hour exclusion.
whyNot.3: Ninety-six hours is longer than needed; 48 hours after the last episode is the standard.

A.q: A nurse is collecting urine from Daisy, 10 months, who has a fever. A clean catch is not possible after several tries. What should the nurse use next?
options: Cotton wool balls in the nappy
A.why: NG224: if a clean catch is not possible, use a urine collection pad; invasive methods come only when non-invasive methods fail.

whyNot.0: Cotton wool balls should not be used to collect urine.
whyNot.2: Gauze should not be used to collect urine.
whyNot.3: Suprapubic aspiration is reserved for when non-invasive methods are not possible.

A.q: Ayla, 8 months, is breastfed and has had diarrhoea for a day. She is alert and feeding with no signs of dehydration. What should the nurse advise?
options: Continue breastfeeding and offer extra fluids
Stop breastfeeding and give ORS for 24 hours
Give diluted apple juice between feeds
A.why: Without dehydration, CG84 advises continuing breastfeeding and other milk feeds and encouraging fluid intake.

whyNot.2: Fruit juice and fizzy drinks should be discouraged.
whyNot.3: 50 mL/kg over 4 hours is the plan for clinical dehydration, which she does not have.

B.q: Josh, 5, has had dysuria and frequency for a day. He is well with a temperature of 37.6°C and no loin pain. A dipstick is positive for leukocyte esterase and nitrite. How should this be classed?
options: Lower UTI to be treated as such
B.why: He has urinary symptoms with a positive dipstick, no fever of 38°C and no loin pain: this is a lower UTI. At 3 years and over a dipstick is as useful as microscopy and culture.

whyNot.0: Upper UTI needs fever of 38°C or more, or loin pain with a lower fever.
whyNot.1: He has symptoms, so this is not asymptomatic bacteriuria.
whyNot.3: None of the atypical features (seriously ill, poor flow, mass, septicaemia) are present.

B.q: Leah, 7 weeks, has a temperature of 38.3°C and is feeding less. The practice nurse obtains a clean catch urine sample. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Dipstick the urine and treat if positive
Send for culture and review the result in 48 hours
Start oral antibiotics while awaiting culture
Refer her immediately to a paediatric specialist
B.why: NG224: babies under 3 months with a possible UTI are referred immediately to a paediatric specialist; with fever they need parenteral antibiotics per NG143.

whyNot.0: Dipstick-led management is not used in babies under 3 months.
whyNot.1: Waiting 48 hours is unsafe in a febrile baby under 3 months.
whyNot.2: Oral antibiotics in the community are not the plan for this age; she needs specialist care.

B.q: Three children on a ward have gastroenteritis. A parent asks what matters most to stop it spreading to her other children at home. What is the best reply?
options: Using alcohol gel after nappy changes
Washing hands with soap and warm water
Wearing gloves when touching the child
Wiping toys with alcohol wipes daily
B.why: CG84: washing hands with soap in warm running water and drying them carefully are the most important factors in preventing spread.

whyNot.0: CG84 names soap and warm running water, not alcohol gel, as the most important measure.
whyNot.2: Gloves do not replace hand hygiene for the family.
whyNot.3: Environmental cleaning helps but is not the most important measure.

C.q: Oscar, 18 months, weighs 10 kg and has gastroenteritis. He is now drowsy, his hands and feet are cold and mottled, and his capillary refill is 5 seconds. What is the immediate fluid plan?
options: IV 5% glucose 200 mL over an hour
C.why: These are signs of shock. CG84: give a rapid IV infusion of 0.9% sodium chloride 10 mL/kg (100 mL for 10 kg), reassess and repeat once if needed.

whyNot.0: Oral rehydration is for dehydration without shock.
whyNot.2: Nasogastric ORS is for dehydration when oral fluids fail, not for shock.
whyNot.3: Glucose solutions are not used as a resuscitation bolus.

C.q: Rania, 6, has fever and vomiting but no urinary symptoms. Her urine dipstick is positive for leukocyte esterase but negative for nitrite. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Send urine for microscopy and culture
Start antibiotics for a presumed UTI
Assume no UTI and look for other causes
C.why: NG224 table 2 (3 years and over): leukocyte esterase positive, nitrite negative: send urine for microscopy and culture, and do not give antibiotics unless there is good clinical evidence of UTI. The leukocytes may reflect an infection elsewhere.

whyNot.1: Without urinary symptoms there is not good clinical evidence of UTI, so antibiotics are not started on this result.
whyNot.2: Repeating the dipstick delays the culture that NG224 recommends.
whyNot.3: That is the plan when both leukocyte esterase and nitrite are negative.

C.q: Max, 4 months, is admitted with a first UTI caused by E. coli. He responds well to antibiotics within 48 hours. What imaging does NG224 recommend?
options: No imaging as he responded well
C.why: NG224: babies under 6 months with a first UTI that responds to treatment have an ultrasound within 6 weeks.

whyNot.0: Ultrasound during the acute infection is for atypical UTI; his is typical.
whyNot.1: Under 6 months, imaging is recommended even with a good response.
whyNot.3: A DMSA scan within 2 weeks is not the routine plan for a typical first UTI.

reteach.title: Fluids in, germs out, urine clean
reteach.question: Which three actions protect a child with gastroenteritis or a possible UTI?

blocks.body: For gastroenteritis: replace what is lost (ORS 50 mL/kg over 4 hours if dehydrated, IV bolus if shocked) and stop the spread (soap and water, 48 hours off). For UTI: get a clean sample (clean catch, then pad) and match the test to the age. The youngest babies, under 3 months, skip the dipstick and go straight to a paediatric specialist.

blocks.text: Cold, mottled hands and a long CRT are shock, not dehydration. Do not keep offering ORS: a shocked child needs a rapid IV bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride 10 mL/kg.

explain.body: For clinical dehydration, give low-osmolarity ORS 50 mL/kg over 4 hours plus maintenance. A 14 kg child needs 700 mL over 4 hours, about 175 mL an hour, offered in small frequent amounts.

items.label: after each large stool once rehydrated, if at risk

test.q: Isaac, 3, weighs 14 kg and has clinical dehydration without shock. What volume of ORS should he receive over 4 hours, as well as maintenance?
test.why: 50 mL/kg x 14 kg = 700 mL over 4 hours, plus maintenance fluids.

whyNot.0: 140 mL is 10 mL/kg, the shock bolus volume, not the ORS deficit.
whyNot.1: 1,400 mL is 100 mL/kg, the IV deficit used for a shocked child.
whyNot.2: 350 mL is 25 mL/kg, half the recommended volume.

explain.body: Decreased consciousness, pale or mottled skin, cold extremities, prolonged CRT, weak pulses or hypotension mean shock. Give 0.9% sodium chloride 10 mL/kg rapidly IV and reassess; repeat once, then consider intensive care.

test.q: Which finding in a child with gastroenteritis suggests shock rather than dehydration alone?
test.why: Cold extremities and pale or mottled skin are signs of clinical shock.

whyNot.0: Sunken eyes are a sign of clinical dehydration.
whyNot.2: Dry mucous membranes are a feature of dehydration.
whyNot.3: Reduced urine output is a feature of dehydration.

explain.body: Clean catch first. If not possible, use a urine collection pad. Never cotton wool, gauze or sanitary towels. Catheter or suprapubic aspiration only if non-invasive methods are not possible. Refrigerate or use boric acid if culture is not within 4 hours.

test.q: A urine sample from a toddler cannot reach the lab for 6 hours. What should the nurse do?
options: Dipstick it and send it later
test.why: NG224: if culture will not happen within 4 hours, refrigerate the sample or use a boric acid container.

whyNot.0: Room temperature allows bacteria to multiply and gives misleading results.
whyNot.3: Dipstick testing does not preserve the sample for culture.

explain.body: Upper UTI (acute pyelonephritis): bacteriuria with fever of 38°C or more, or a lower fever with loin pain. Lower UTI (cystitis): bacteriuria without systemic features. Do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria.

test.q: Sofia, 9, has a temperature of 37.8°C, a positive urine culture and pain in her right loin. How should this be classed?
options: Not a UTI as fever is under 38°C
test.why: Bacteriuria with a fever below 38°C plus loin pain is an upper UTI.

whyNot.0: Loin pain makes this an upper, not a lower, UTI.
whyNot.1: She has symptoms, so this is not asymptomatic.
whyNot.3: Loin pain with a lower fever still meets the upper UTI definition.
